title: or says /or/
parentNote: This is the second bossy r. Two days ago the r got hold of an a and made ar; today it does the same to an o and the pair say or, as in fork, corn and storm. Two slips turn up here. The first is the a hanging about from last week, so corn comes out carn — say the pair yourself, car and corn, and let your child hear the swap. The second is sounding the letters one at a time, so fork becomes fo-ruk; point at the or as one chunk, the way you did with ar. Round your lips into a little o and let the r roll off the end. Today also quietly unlocks "for", which your child has been unable to read for sixty-three days and will now meet everywhere.

activities.mouthCue: Round your lips into a little o, then let the r roll off the end: or.
activities.prompt: Another team where the r is in charge. The o has given up its everyday sound.
Two of these have an r bossing a vowel. Listen for which vowel is under it.
Three ways to use an o, and all three say something different.
Only two sounds in this one, and the or is one of them. You have wanted this word for weeks.
The longest one. Five sounds and two bits: say mor, then ning, then push them together.
All three start the same. Listen right to the end.
Two have an o under the r and one has an a. Listen to the middle, then the end.
Two of these are the same until the very last sound.

activities.text: Mark got a big fork for the hot corn.
In the morning a storm came, and the corn is flat.
Is that a horn, or is it a stork?

activities.title: The stork in the storm
activities.prompt: Read the story one line at a time. Tap any word you want to hear again.
lines: A big storm hit the farm in the morning.
Mark ran for the porch, and Meg ran for the barn.
The corn is flat, and the red flag is torn.
Then Mark did spot a stork stuck in the thorns.
It can not get free, and it did honk and honk.
Meg got a fork and did lift the thorns up.
The stork got free and did land on the porch.
Mark did grin. The storm got the corn, and they got a stork!
